text: 1 Overview

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.1 What is multiomeR?
multiomeR is a targets-based workflow for processing and analyzing single-nucleus 10x Genomics Multiome datasets.
The workflow starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes RNA and ATAC data, builds multimodal aggregations, and supports optional downstream modules for differential analyses and human genetic enrichment.
multiomeR is currently in beta. It is meant to be adapted to your own data, compute setup, and biological questions, while keeping the shared workflow as lean and readable as possible.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.2 Why use it?

Adaptable framework: The repository is meant to be modified through config files, target selections, helper functions, and optional modules.
Transparent execution: Each processing and analysis step is represented as an explicit targets target.
Efficient reruns: targets reruns only the parts of the workflow affected by changed inputs, code, or config.
Multimodal analysis: The main pipeline covers RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, WNN integration, and optional downstream modules.

The framework assumes some familiarity with R and targets, but the public example workflow is intended to provide a concrete starting point.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.3 Workflow at a glance
multiomeR is organized around one main pipeline and optional downstream modules.
The main pipeline is the workflow most users run first. It starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes each 10x reaction, aggregates selected reactions, and builds multimodal RNA/ATAC outputs for clustering, cell typing, and WNN integration.
The modules are optional branches that run from configured aggregations. Enable them only when the relevant input data and biological question are present.



Flowchart of the sample processing pipeline

title: 2  Using this manual
text:
2.2 Terminology
The following nomenclature is used in the documentation and code:

‘10x reaction’ (or possibly just ‘reaction’): The experimental/computational outcome of a single lane on the 10x Genomics Controller chip, which might contain nuclei from multiple samples and/or multiple donors/individuals. One 10x reaction thus corresponds to a single output directory from cellranger-arc count.
donor: A single individual, subject, patient, participant, etc. that has a unique donor_id and specific genotype.
dataset: A group of one or more reactions that share dataset-level processing settings, such as reference genome and reaction-level QC filters.
aggregation: A configured joint analysis of one or more reactions, including merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, and optional downstream modules.

title: 3  Installation
section: 3.3 Create and launch the pixi environment
text:
3.3 Create and launch the pixi environment
If pixi is not installed yet, install it first:


Bash

curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"

Install the pixi environment from the repository root (<5 mins):


Bash

pixi install --run-post-link-scripts

Start an interactive R session inside the pixi environment:


Bash

pixi shell
R

Use this repository-root R session as the evaluation environment for subsequent R commands in this manual.






NoteWhy pixi?





multiomeR depends on both R packages and command-line genomics tools. Pixi keeps those dependencies in one locked environment, so R, Bioconductor packages, and external tools such as macs3, tabix, and cellsnp-lite are resolved together instead of being installed manually across separate package managers.









NoteWhy is --run-post-link-scripts needed?





The --run-post-link-scripts flag is required for Bioconductor data packages such as the BSgenome genome packages. Pixi disables conda post-link scripts by default, but these packages use Bioconda’s post-link scripts to materialize the actual R package directories in the pixi environment.

title: 5  Outputs
text:
5.2 Files
Other targets in the pipeline explicitly writes files to disk inside tarchetypes::tar_file() targets. These targets can still be loaded by targets::tar_read(), but their value is simply the file path rather than an in-memory analysis object.


R

targets::tar_read(cellranger_barcodes_tsv.healthy_PBMC_human)
targets::tar_read(aggregated_GEX_BPCells_matrix_dir.GEX.immune_human_2x)
targets::tar_read(consensus_peak_BED.ATAC.immune_human_2x)

Internally, these paths are created with get_structured_file_path(). The helper derives a stable location from the active target name and writes it under outputs/files. Target name parts after dots become parent directories in reverse order, so a target like aggregated_GEX_BPCells_matrix_dir.GEX.immune_human_2x is placed under:
outputs/files/immune_human_2x/GEX/
After the public demo run, you should therefore find produced files ordered separated by individual reactions, datasets, and the aggregation name:
outputs/files/
|-- healthy_PBMC_human/ (reaction 1 specific files)
|-- lymphoma_lymph_human/ (reaction 2 specific files)
`-- immune_human_2x/ (aggregation-level files)
Please see the official targets documentation for more info on working with external files: insert link to most relevant manual page(s)

title: 6  Overview
text:
6.1 Purpose
This workflow is defined in _targets.R and represents the main analysis pipeline after Cell Ranger output generation. It processes individual 10x reactions in parallel, combines selected reactions into aggregations, and runs several multimodal workflows.
Representative outputs from the public example workflow are collected in the main pipeline output gallery.

title: 6  Overview
text:
6.2 Features
The main pipeline features:

per-reaction QC and optional preprocessing before aggregation
BPCells-native RNA and ATAC processing
GEX, ATAC, and WNN clustering and review checkpoints
cell type annotation, marker summaries, coverage tracks, and multimodal output objects
optional subgroup reprocessing for sufficiently large parent groups

title: 6  Overview
text:
6.3 Configuration layers
The main pipeline is configured in three layers: datasets define shared genome and QC settings, reactions point to individual 10x outputs, and aggregations choose which reactions to process together.
Each YAML file has a default entry with shared parameters. Named datasets and aggregations inherit from default unless they declare another inherits parent, so template entries usually only list required values and settings that intentionally differ from the defaults.

title: 7  Configuration and inputs
text:
7.3 cfg_aggregations.yaml
Aggregation-level settings live in cfg_aggregations.yaml. An aggregation combines one or more configured reactions and controls merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, annotation, plotting, and optional downstream modules.
At minimum, each aggregation needs:







Field
Meaning




aggregation_reaction_IDs
Reaction IDs from cfg_reactions.tsv to include in the joint analysis.


aggregation_GEX_marker_genes
Named marker-gene lists used for module scoring and cluster annotation.


aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv
Donor-level metadata table with a donor_id column.


aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv
Reaction-level metadata table with a TENX_reaction_ID column.



Optional aggregation settings control QC filters, RNA and ATAC dimensions, clustering resolution, UMAP parameters, subgroup analysis, plotting variables, track export, and enabled modules. YAML entries are divided into mandatory parameters that must be set and optional parameters that are usually inherited from default unless the entry overrides them. NULL values intentionally disable optional behavior.
Each aggregation also points to metadata files:

aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv: donor-level metadata with a donor_id column matching the donor IDs assigned during per-reaction processing.
aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv: reaction-level metadata with a TENX_reaction_ID column matching the configured reaction IDs.

These metadata tables are joined to the per-cell metadata before downstream correction, plotting, and modelling.
The public PBMC aggregation below is rendered directly from cfg_aggregations.yaml. It shows the required aggregation inputs plus the example-specific optional overrides; standard optional settings are inherited from default.


Show immune_human_2x

    aggregation_reaction_IDs: [healthy_PBMC_human, lymphoma_lymph_human]
    aggregation_GEX_marker_genes:

      NK: [KLRD1, KLRC1, KLRF1, NKG7, GNLY]
      Mono: [CD14, FCGR3A, LYZ, S100A8, S100A9]

title: 11  Performance overview
text:
multiomeR is built on targets, which represents the workflow as a dependency graph. This makes the pipeline naturally parallelizable: whenever two targets do not depend on each other, targets can schedule them independently through the configured execution backend.
In practice, this is why reaction-level work, aggregation-level branches, and optional downstream modules can often run in parallel. The exact amount of parallelism depends on the active target selection, available workers, file-system throughput, and the controller setup described in Distributed computing.


R

targets::tar_make()

The command above asks targets to build every outdated target. targets then follows the dependency graph, skips up-to-date work, and dispatches independent branches according to the configured controller.

title: 12  Distributed computing
text:
12.1 Controller contract
multiomeR runs targets through the targets and crew backend. The repository ships with crew_controllers.R pointing to a local-controller setup, which is sufficient for the public PBMC demo.
For larger datasets, adapt crew_controllers.R to match your scheduler, queue names, resource limits, and worker startup requirements.
crew_controllers.R must return a named list with:
Targets request resources by cores, RAM, and optionally GPUs through get_tar_resources(). The first row of controller_resources_tibble is the default controller, and row order controls which matching controller is preferred. GPU controllers are excluded unless gpus_req > 0.

title: 12  Distributed computing
text:
controller_list: the list of crew controllers.
controller_resources_tibble: a table with controller_name, cores, RAM_GB, and gpus.

title: 12  Distributed computing
text:
12.2 Local default
The default template uses a local crew controller:


Bash

crew_controllers.R -> crew_controllers_template.R

Increase local workers, cores, and memory only after the example workflow succeeds on your machine.

title: 12  Distributed computing
text:
12.3 Cluster execution
For cluster execution, replace the local controller with a scheduler-backed controller such as crew.cluster::crew_controller_slurm(). Keep the controller_resources_tibble rows aligned with the controller names, because that table controls how target-level resource requests are routed.
